about: Lesson F9's own inputs: how the Sankey's sectors group, the colours of its nodes, who typically decides what in U.S. energy (each claim with a dated primary source), and the numbers to remember. Prairie City's flows are read from prairie-city.json (flows, balance, supply), never copied here.

actors.label: The city
actors.sub: council, permits, its own buildings and buses
actors.levers: Energy codes for new buildings and the permits that enforce them, rooftop-solar permits, its own buses and buildings.

actors.label: The utility
actors.sub: electricity and, here, gas: wires, mains, power supply
actors.levers: Distribution wires and substations, gas mains, and, in Kansas, its own power plants and contracts.

actors.label: The state regulator
actors.levers: The rates and terms of investor-owned electricity and gas utilities, and a review of their costs.

actors.label: Owners
actors.sub: households, businesses, the plants and the campus
actors.levers: What to install, which car to buy and how to use them: furnaces, heat pumps, vehicles, processes.

actors.label: Federal rules
actors.sub: grid markets, equipment, pipelines, fuel economy
actors.levers: Interstate transmission, wholesale power and gas pipelines ([[ferc|FERC]]); efficiency standards for equipment sold (the Department of Energy); pipeline safety and fuel economy (Transportation Department agencies).

levers.text: The price per kWh a home pays its investor-owned electric utility
levers.why: Typically the [[public-utility-commission|state commission]] sets or approves [[investor-owned-utility|investor-owned utilities']] rates; in Kansas, the Kansas Corporation Commission.

levers.text: Which plants the utility owns and which electricity contracts it signs
levers.why: Where utilities are [[vertically-integrated-utility|vertically integrated]], as in Kansas, the utility builds, owns or buys its supply; the regulator reviews the costs. [[spp|SPP]]'s market decides which plants run.

levers.text: The substations and feeders that serve each street
levers.why: Local electric utilities operate the distribution system and plan for future needs.

levers.text: Rules for interstate transmission and for electricity sold to utilities for resale
levers.why: [[ferc|FERC]] regulates the transmission and [[wholesale-price|wholesale sale]] of electricity in interstate commerce.

levers.text: The least efficiency a new furnace, water heater or light bulb may have
levers.why: DOE sets efficiency standards for more than 70 kinds of appliances and equipment.

levers.text: Safety rules for the gas mains under the streets
levers.why: PHMSA, the federal pipeline-safety agency, writes the safety rules; certified state programs inspect most gas distribution pipelines.

levers.text: The minimum energy rules new buildings in Prairie City must meet (the energy code)
levers.why: Kansas leaves the [[building-code|energy code]] to each city or county (home rule), and local permit offices enforce it; in many states the state adopts one code.

levers.text: A permit to put solar panels on a roof
levers.why: Local governments issue the permits for rooftop solar.

levers.text: Whether a home swaps its furnace for a heat pump
levers.why: The owner chooses, within federal efficiency standards and local codes; DOE's guide is written for that choice.

roles.note: Roles for a Kansas city served by an investor-owned utility. Typical U.S. roles, not universal: they differ by state, and a city that owns its utility answers to its own local government.

muni.q: Some U.S. cities own their electric utility. If Prairie City did, which lever would move to its own local government?

feedback.rates: Public power utilities are generally regulated by their own local government, not the state; Kansas's commission does not regulate most of them.
feedback.standards: Equipment standards stay federal (DOE) whoever owns the utility; the rates are what move: public power answers to its own local government.
feedback.wholesale: Interstate transmission stays with FERC whoever owns the utility; the rates are what move: public power answers to its own local government.

muni.extra: In 2017, 1,958 publicly owned utilities served about 12,100 customers each on average (EIA).

facts.what: U.S. electricity customers served by investor-owned utilities (72% in 2017); 1,958 publicly owned utilities served about 12,100 customers each on average.
